drafts.after: First principle: conditional immortality. The endless life is a gift God gives. We do not have it by ourselves. The living know that they shall die. The dead know not anything. They have no more a portion in anything done under the sun. Psalm 146:4 agrees: "his breath goeth forth... in that very day his thoughts perish". So death is an unconscious sleep. The word nephesh means the whole living person. That person comes apart at death. The dead wait asleep for the physical resurrection at Christ's return. The serpent said, "Ye shall not surely die". The whole Bible proves that lie false.
drafts.reason: Defines the technical labels in place ('conditional immortality', and the transliteration nephesh) and replaces 'Scripture reveals' and 'the harmonious testimony of the entire canon' with plain words. The 26-word sentence and the semicolon clause are split into one-idea sentences. Both KJV quotations and the Psalm 146:4 citation are byte-identical; the lowercase 'his' opening the quote is kept exactly as the source has it. QUOTE-REVIEW: his breath goeth forth... in that very day his thoughts perish vs His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish (Psalm 146:4) — the difference is the capital letter on the first word only, because the source quotes the line mid-sentence; no word of the reading differs, and the quotation is left byte-identical.

drafts.after: You are going to the grave. In that place there is no work and no knowledge. First principle: the grave is silent. Do your work while you are alive. Work belongs to the daylight. It does not belong to the dark place after death.
drafts.reason: Gives the opening KJV-echo clause a subject and a verb, and replaces the abstract 'the urgency of diligence' and 'the dark hereafter' with everyday wording. The em-dash clause that carried a second idea is now two short sentences.

drafts.after: Dust to dust. First principle: at death a man goes two ways. His body goes back to the soil. His spirit goes back to God who gave it. This is Genesis 2:7 in reverse.
drafts.reason: Splits the semicolon and the em-dash into one-idea sentences, and says plainly what 'the twofold destiny of man' and 'Genesis 2:7 in reverse' mean. The Genesis 2:7 citation is unchanged.

drafts.after: There is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not. First principle: nobody on earth does good all the time. That is the wisdom book's plain word on sin. Romans 3 builds a chain of verses that say no one is righteous. This line is part of that chain.
drafts.reason: Replaces 'catena' with 'chain' and explains it in place, and turns 'the universal-sin text of the wisdom canon' into a plain sentence a reader does not have to decode. The Romans 3 reference is kept.

drafts.after: God will bring every work into judgment, including every secret thing, good or evil. First principle: nothing hidden escapes that day. Paul and John both say the same thing about it.
drafts.reason: 'No classified compartment escapes' and 'quote the same audit' become plain words. Paul and John, and the good-or-evil distinction, are kept, and each sentence carries one idea.

drafts.after: God shall judge the righteous and the wicked. First principle: there is a time for every purpose and for every work. The Preacher saw injustice all around him. He held on to this promise. God's courtroom is still coming.
drafts.reason: The em-dash and the colon-plus-semicolon are split into short sentences, and 'the Preacher's consolation under injustice' and 'the schedule includes a courtroom' are said in everyday words.

drafts.after: Fear God, and keep his commandments. First principle: this is the whole duty of man. Everything here passes like a breath. Two things still stand. We are to fear God. We are to obey him.
drafts.reason: 'Vanity' used as a bare abstraction is replaced by what the word means here (everything passes like a breath), and 'reverent fear and obedient keeping' becomes two plain sentences so the conclusion is not tidied into a slogan.

drafts.after: A dead person knows nothing at all. Every thought stops until the resurrection.
drafts.reason: 'Absolute unconsciousness' and 'complete cessation of mental existence' are words the reader must decode; the semicolon is split and the resurrection is still named.

drafts.after: This is the hope the apostles taught. When Christ comes the second time, people hear him and see him. Then all believers wake from sleep together.
drafts.reason: The telegraphic label 'The apostolic hope' becomes a sentence with a subject and verb, and the relative clause 'which is heard and seen' plus the passive 'are woken' become active sentences naming who acts.

drafts.after: After the fall, death works like this. The body goes back to dust. The breath goes back to God.
drafts.reason: Drops the bare 'The fall:' label and splits the 'and' chain so each sentence carries one idea.

drafts.after: This is how God made man at creation. Man does not have a soul that lives on by itself. The man became a living soul.
drafts.reason: The label 'The creation formula' becomes a sentence, and the two statements are separated so the KJV-echo clause stands on its own with a subject and verb.

drafts.after: God clears sin, death, and the grave out of his universe. He destroys them forever.
drafts.reason: The colon label becomes a second active sentence naming God as the one who acts, and 'cleans up' becomes the plainer 'clears ... out'.

drafts.after: The Bible agrees. In death a person is not aware of anything. No one praises God there. No one speaks to anyone there.
drafts.reason: The 'Scripture agrees:' label becomes a short sentence, and the three abstract nouns (awareness, praise, communication) become three plain statements with subjects.

drafts.after: This is when the change happens. God makes the body unable to decay at the resurrection. That change does not happen at death.
drafts.reason: The passive 'is made incorruptible' becomes an active sentence naming God, and 'incorruptible' is replaced by everyday words.

drafts.after: Death and hell are cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.
drafts.reason: The em-dash title is split into the two statements it compresses, and the verb 'are' is added so the first half is a real sentence. 'Death and hell', 'the lake of fire' and 'the second death' are kept.

drafts.after: The dead in Christ shall rise first. That happens when the Lord comes down.
drafts.reason: The telegraphic tail 'at the Lord's descent' gets a subject and a verb, and 'descent' becomes everyday words. 'The dead in Christ shall rise first' is kept word for word.

drafts.after: Dust plus the breath of life makes a living soul. The Hebrew words for that are nephesh chayah.
drafts.reason: The '+ / =' formula becomes a sentence, and the transliteration nephesh chayah is kept byte-identical with a plain gloss around it instead of inside an equation.

drafts.after: His breath goes out. In that very day his thoughts stop.
drafts.reason: Splits the semicolon clause and replaces 'goeth forth' and 'perish' with everyday words. This title was not a verbatim KJV clause, since it dropped 'His' from the front of the line.

drafts.after: The dead know nothing at all. In the grave no one can plan anything.
drafts.reason: Splits the semicolon and turns the fragment 'no device in the grave' into a sentence with a subject and a verb.

drafts.after: This is where the chain starts. Only God lives forever on his own. We live forever only if God gives us that life.
drafts.reason: The 'The starting point:' label becomes a sentence, and 'it is conditional' is said in plain words with God named as the one who gives.

drafts.after: The mortal body puts on immortality at the last trump. The last trump is the final trumpet blast.
drafts.reason: The telegraphic 'Mortal puts on immortality' gets a subject, and 'the last trump' is defined in the next sentence instead of being left as a label.

drafts.after: God burns the wicked to stubble. They become ashes under your feet.
drafts.reason: Names God as the one who acts, and gives the fragment 'become ashes under feet' a subject. 'Stubble' and 'ashes' are kept, and second person is used as the verse itself does.

drafts.after: This is what Christ taught. He said, "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth... Lazarus is dead."
drafts.reason: The fragment 'Christ's teaching:' becomes a sentence with a subject and a verb, so the reader is told who taught and that he spoke. The KJV quotation is kept byte-identical, including the ellipsis and the period inside the closing quote.
